const r = await tools.exec_command({cmd:"cat > /tmp/exposed-light-design-luna.md <<'EOF'
# Candidate: system-resolved theme state over shared semantic tokens

## Caller usage

The application has no theme control. It follows the visitor's operating-system preference, while all pages and shared UI components keep using the same semantic tokens.

```css
.panel { color: var(--text); background: var(--surface); }
.member-page { --accent: var(--accent-member); }
.funder-page { --accent: var(--accent-funder); }
```

The document exposes one resolved state, `data-theme="light"` or `data-theme="dark"`. The state selects a palette; it does not change page or entity identity.

## Data shape and ownership

```ts
type Theme = "light" | "dark";

function resolveTheme(prefersLight: boolean): Theme;
function applyTheme(root: HTMLElement, theme: Theme): void;
```

`resolveTheme` maps the browser's system preference to the finite theme vocabulary. The root document owns the applied state. The design system owns the token values in `frontend/src/lib/ui/tokens.css`; components consume semantic tokens and never branch on the theme. Keep `--accent-member` and `--accent-funder` as identity tokens, with `--accent` as the existing per-page alias. Keep party chart colors in their existing category palette, outside the surface theme palette, so a background change cannot recolor party identity.

The resolved state has only two values because there is no user override or manual switch in scope. If a switch is added later, model the preference separately as `"system" | "light" | "dark"` and derive `Theme`; do not conflate a stored preference with the active palette.

## Application shape

`frontend/src/lib/ui/tokens.css` defines the complete dark palette on `:root` and the light palette under `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Include surface, canvas, text, muted text, lines, warning, action ink, focus, and any remaining hard-coded surface colors as semantic tokens. `base.css` uses `color-scheme: light dark` only if supported consistently; preferably set `color-scheme: light` or `dark` from the selected root theme so native controls match.

A small browser-only resolver in `frontend/src/lib/theme.ts` reads `matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: light)")`, calls `applyTheme`, and listens for preference changes. Install it from `hooks.client.ts`, which already owns browser initialization. It writes the same root attribute idempotently. Do not persist anything because there is no user-selected preference.

## First paint and SSR

SSR cannot know the visitor's OS preference, so an explicit JS-resolved attribute risks a dark server render followed by a light repaint. For first paint, put the palette values behind the CSS media query as a bootstrap: light preference selects the light token block immediately, with dark as the default. The client resolver then stamps the corresponding `data-theme` state before normal interaction and tracks live system changes. This keeps first paint correct without consulting browser APIs during SSR. The two CSS selectors must share the same palette declarations or generated token source; avoid separately maintaining a media-query palette and a data-attribute palette by making the early selector a grouped selector (`:root[data-theme="light"], @media ...`) where practical, or prefer CSS-only media queries if the build constraints make shared declarations awkward.

## Tradeoff against CSS-only media queries

CSS-only `@media (prefers-color-scheme: light)` is the smallest and most reliable option for this exact requirement: it paints correctly before JavaScript, works with SSR, and handles OS changes automatically. It should be the implementation if no other code needs to observe the selected theme.

The explicit `data-theme` state gives scripts and diagnostics a canonical resolved value and leaves a clean extension point for a future override. It adds a browser resolver, an OS-change listener, and the risk of duplicated palette selectors or a flash if the CSS bootstrap is omitted. With no manual switch requested, that benefit is modest; preserve the explicit state only if another existing consumer needs to inspect theme. Otherwise use the same semantic tokens with CSS media queries alone and omit the TypeScript state layer.

## Verification

Use the existing `/design-system` gallery and representative landing, MP, funder, and party-chart views. In browser verification, emulate both `prefers-color-scheme` values and assert readable text, surfaces, borders, focus indicators, form controls, and chart labels. Confirm MP purple, funder teal, and party category colors remain stable across both themes. Check the initial HTML/CSS paint with JavaScript disabled, then enable JavaScript and change the emulated preference to verify no visible transition or stale state. Run the frontend check, production build, and affected Playwright tests when implementing.
EOF
","yield_time_ms":10000,"max_output_tokens":1000});
